lesson.title: Rank rows without collapsing them

lead.text: GROUP BY collapses rows into groups. A window function does not: it adds a value beside each row.
OVER (ORDER BY ...) sets the order it uses. ROW_NUMBER numbers each row separately. RANK and DENSE_RANK give tied rows the same number.

steps.headline: A window function adds a value to each row and keeps every row.

lead.text: One query groups the known amounts. The other adds a window calculation. Compare what each does to the rows.

reveal.text: You saw what the window version kept: the individual rows. The grouped version collapsed them into one row per amount.

queries.label: Query A
queries.sql: SELECT amount, COUNT(*) AS orders FROM orders WHERE amount IS NOT NULL GROUP BY amount ORDER BY amount DESC;

queries.label: Query B
queries.sql: SELECT id, amount, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY amount DESC, id ASC) AS position FROM orders WHERE amount IS NOT NULL ORDER BY amount DESC, id ASC;

steps.headline: Rank the orders by customer_id with RANK.

queries.label: Rank with RANK
queries.sql: SELECT id, customer_id, RANK() OVER (ORDER BY customer_id) AS position FROM orders ORDER BY customer_id, id;

queries.label: Number with ROW_NUMBER
queries.sql: SELECT id, customer_id, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY customer_id, id) AS position FROM orders ORDER BY customer_id, id;

workedSteps.text: The next rank is one more than the number of rows before it.
workedSteps.math: order 103: two rows before, so rank 3

lead.text: Order the amounts largest first. For RANK, count the rows that come before the amount you are asked about.

reveal.text: You counted the rows ahead and added one. Ties are part of that count, which is why RANK can leave gaps.

queries.label: Number each row
queries.sql: SELECT id, amount, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY amount DESC, id ASC) AS position FROM orders WHERE amount IS NOT NULL ORDER BY amount DESC, id ASC;

queries.label: Share ranks for equal amounts
queries.sql: SELECT id, amount, RANK() OVER (ORDER BY amount DESC) AS position FROM orders WHERE amount IS NOT NULL ORDER BY amount DESC, id ASC;

lead.text: DENSE_RANK also gives tied rows the same rank. It never skips: the next different amount takes the next integer.

reveal.text: You counted different amounts, not rows. Choose RANK or DENSE_RANK by what the report should mean.

queries.label: Ranks with gaps
queries.sql: SELECT id, amount, RANK() OVER (ORDER BY amount DESC) AS position FROM orders WHERE amount IS NOT NULL ORDER BY amount DESC, id ASC;

queries.label: Ranks without gaps
queries.sql: SELECT id, amount, DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY amount DESC) AS position FROM orders WHERE amount IS NOT NULL ORDER BY amount DESC, id ASC;

lead.text: The window ranks by everything inside OVER (ORDER BY ...). Think about what a second column does to a tie.

queries.label: Rank the amount
queries.sql: SELECT id, amount, RANK() OVER (ORDER BY amount DESC) AS position FROM orders WHERE amount IS NOT NULL ORDER BY amount DESC, id ASC;

queries.label: Rank amount and id
queries.sql: SELECT id, amount, RANK() OVER (ORDER BY amount DESC, id ASC) AS position FROM orders WHERE amount IS NOT NULL ORDER BY amount DESC, id ASC;

lesson.orientation: Distinguish ROW_NUMBER, RANK and DENSE_RANK and choose tie behaviour deliberately.
lesson.nextAction: Apply the idea to the next query.

blocks.text: Four runners finish in 10, 10, 12 and 14 seconds. Runners with equal times share a place.

intro.promise: By the end you'll rank rows with ROW_NUMBER, RANK or DENSE_RANK and say what happens to ties.

recap.keyIdea: A window function ranks rows without collapsing them. ROW_NUMBER never ties. RANK leaves gaps after ties, and DENSE_RANK does not.

blocks.text: You placed the 14-second runner 4th, then ranked the amount 40 as 3 with RANK and 2 with DENSE_RANK.

recap.nextHook: Next, restart the numbering inside each partition.

questions.prompt: What does a window calculation preserve here?
hints: Compare the five-row window result with the grouped result.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A window calculation adds a result to each retained order row. Unlike GROUP BY aggregation, it does not collapse the rows into one row per group.

questions.onCorrect: Each individual known order row. A window calculation adds a value without collapsing rows.

misconceptions.feedback: That is what GROUP BY does. A window calculation keeps the rows.
Nothing is filtered out. Every known order stays.

questions.prompt: Under RANK() OVER (ORDER BY amount DESC), what rank does the amount 40 receive?
hints: Count rows with greater amounts.
Ordinary rank is one plus the number of preceding higher-valued rows.
Ordinary rank equals one plus the number of rows whose amount is greater.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Two 80 rows share rank 1, so the next row's rank is 3.

questions.onCorrect: 3. Two rows have a greater amount, so RANK is one plus that count.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the dense rank. RANK counts the rows that come before, ties included.
Count how many rows have a greater amount, then add one.

questions.prompt: Under DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY amount DESC), what rank does the amount 40 receive?
hints: Dense ranks count different preceding values.
There is one distinct amount greater than forty.
Dense rank equals one plus the number of distinct greater amount values.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 80 is the first distinct amount; 40 is the second.

questions.onCorrect: 2. One different amount is greater, so DENSE_RANK is one plus that count.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the plain rank. Dense ranks count different values.

questions.prompt: What happens to the 80 tie if id is added inside the ranking window's ORDER BY?
hints: The window compares the complete ordering tuple.

acceptedIdeas: The two rows no longer tie
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Window ties depend on every ORDER BY expression. Adding distinct ids makes the two 80 rows different ordering keys, so they no longer tie.

choices.label: The two rows no longer tie
Both rows must still have rank 1

questions.onCorrect: The two rows no longer tie. Adding id makes every order different in the window.

misconceptions.feedback: The window now compares id too, so the amounts no longer tie.

questions.prompt: Amounts sorted descending are 90, 90, 70, 50. What is RANK for 70?
hints: Ordinary rank includes gaps after ties.
There are two preceding higher-valued rows.
Count the two rows with 90, then add one for the next row's ordinary rank.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Two higher rows precede 70, so its ordinary rank is 3.

questions.onCorrect: 3. Two rows with 90 come before it, so RANK is one more than that.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts only the different greater values. RANK counts rows ahead.
Count the rows with a greater amount, then add one.

questions.prompt: Type the function name that gives every row a separate position in the specified order.
hints: This function assigns consecutive positions even when values tie.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: ROW_NUMBER assigns a separate consecutive position to every row in the window's specified order. A unique tie-breaker makes that order deterministic.

questions.onCorrect: ROW_NUMBER. It gives every row its own consecutive position.

misconceptions.feedback: That gives tied rows the same position. The one wanted separates every row.

questions.prompt: What place does the 14-second runner get?
hints: Two runners share first place.
How many runners finished ahead of the 14-second runner?
Add one to the number of runners ahead.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Two runners tie for first, and one more finishes ahead of the 14-second runner. Three runners are ahead, so fourth place.

questions.onCorrect: 4. A place counts the runners ahead of you, ties included. RANK works the same way.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts the different times. A place counts the runners who finished ahead.

questions.prompt: The amounts are 30, 10 and 20. With ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY amount DESC), which amount gets number 1?
hints: Which direction does DESC use?
The first row in the stated order gets number 1.
Which amount comes first, largest first?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: DESC puts the largest amount first, so 30 is numbered 1.

questions.onCorrect: 30. The ORDER BY inside OVER sets the order, and the first row in that order gets number 1.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the smallest. DESC puts the largest first.

questions.prompt: Why does order 103 get rank 3 and not 2?
hints: How many rows come before order 103?

acceptedIdeas: Two rows come before it, so its rank is one more than that.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Orders 101 and 102 come before it, so its rank is two plus one.

questions.onCorrect: RANK is one plus the number of rows that come before, ties included.

choices.label: Two rows come before it, so its rank is one more than that.
Rank counts the different customer ids only.

misconceptions.feedback: RANK counts rows ahead, not different values.
Ranks are not used up. A rank comes from how many rows are ahead.

questions.prompt: Amounts sorted descending are 90, 90, 70 and 50. What is DENSE_RANK for 70?
hints: DENSE_RANK never skips a number.
How many different amounts are greater than 70?
Add one to the number of different greater values.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: One different amount, 90, is greater than 70. Dense rank counts values, so it is one plus one.

questions.onCorrect: 2. DENSE_RANK counts different greater values, so tied rows do not push the next rank up.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the plain RANK, which counts rows ahead. DENSE_RANK counts different values.
